Favour of Credit Growth: The RBI's 125bps repo rate reduction through CY2025 marks the most aggressive easing cycle India has seen since the COVID response, bringing the benchmark rate to 5.25%. Simultaneously, the 100bps CRR cut to 3% released approximately ₹2.5 lakh crore of durable liquidity into the banking system, directly expanding the lendable resource base for banks and NBFCs. 

Moreover, GST 2.0's simplification from a four-tier to a two-tier structure increases effective household disposable income, particularly in the consumption-heavy middle class, directly translating into higher credit absorption capacity. The combination of monetary easing and fiscal rationalisation is boosting credit, and financial intermediaries are the primary beneficiaries.

Sub-Themes:
Microfinance: the sector endured a sharp asset quality deterioration through FY25 driven by borrower over-leveraging and collection breakdowns, but as of early 2026 PAR metrics are moderating and new disbursements are performing materially better under tighter regulatory guardrails (₹2 lakh borrower cap, three-lender limit). 

In gold loans: record domestic gold prices have expanded loan eligibility under the 75% LTV cap, driving gold loan AUM up 42% YoY to ₹15.6 trillion — a structural tailwind for Muthoot, Manappuram, and bank-run gold loan portfolios. 

Vehicle finance: the GST restructuring on automobiles drove a 20% YoY volume surge in late 2025, directly expanding auto loan origination pipelines. 

Housing finance: 2 years of volume consolidation driven by affordability fatigue is expected to reverse as the 125bps rate cut meaningfully reduces EMI burden on ₹50–80 lakh ticket-size buyers who were the most rate-sensitive. 

Business loan: India's formalising SME and startup ecosystem continues to structurally drive working capital and business loan demand, particularly in Tier II/III cities with limited institutional credit penetration.

Valuations:
Large-cap private banks and select NBFCs are trading at valuations of the prior stress cycle (covid), offering a nice entry point with favourable valuation cushion.

El Niño / Monsoon Risk: Multiple meteorological agencies including Skymet, IMD, and WMO are flagging an evolving El Niño with ~60% probability of below-normal monsoon from June 2026 onwards; historically, weak monsoons compress rural incomes, delay agricultural loan repayments, and elevate stress in kisan credit card portfolios and MFI books concentrated in rain-dependent geographies

Inflationary Reversal / Rate Risk: Sustained geopolitical tensions in energy markets could push crude prices higher, spill into domestic CPI via fuel and transport costs, and force a hike in RBI REPO rates, compressing NIMs across the sector

Deposit Stress: Rising SIP inflows — now running at record monthly levels above ~₹25,000 crore — reflect a structural shift in household savings away from bank fixed deposits and into equity mutual funds; this reduces the low-cost, stable deposit base that banks have historically relied upon to fund credit growth, and if the trend accelerates, it could tighten the liability side of bank balance sheets even as loan demand picks up, compressing the credit-deposit ratio and pressuring funding costs.

IT sector, hugely dependent on humans to design and develop softaware (write codes), felt business contraction risk with investors lowering the terminal growth rate assumptions. This triggered broad-based selling across IT stocks. I view this as fear-driven selling, because over the long run, IT companies stand to benefit — provided they successfully pivot train people for prompt engineering and Agentic AI innovation.

AI, no doubt, is going to stay here and disrupt tarditional workflows and tasks. Recalling the 'Dot-com' bubble, technology stays, but the companies boasting about their tech-led product may not. A similar situation may occur with AI. AI capex by big U.S. tech comapnies is now bigger than all countries' military spend(ex. U.S) at $424 bn (~₹40L crs), increasing at 32% CAGR for 6 yrs. To maintain their lead in the AI race, U.S. hyperscalers are deploying significant free cash flows and taking on debt — yet return visibility on these investments remains limited.

On the flows side, FIIs have net sold $32.7 billion in Indian equities since October 2024, rotating into undervalued emerging markets and AI-theme plays globally. However, when earnings visibility in those bets deteriorates, India could see a reversal of these outflows.

From a technical standpoint, the IT sector has corrected ~35% over 15 months. Historically, 30–50% drawdowns have been followed by average forward returns exceeding 50%, with a 92% probability of positive returns over a two-year horizon(A DSP MF study). The sector currently sits in oversold territory (14-day RSI below 20) and appears fairly to slightly undervalued on fundamental metrics. Notably, promoter buying has been observed in select IT names — a constructive signal.

What keeps Digital India running is electricity. Demand growth is driven by multiple factors: 
1. Rising temperatures pushing AC penetration (India at ~10% vs. 60%+ in China vs. 90%+ in developed economies)
2. EV adoption demanding more electricity consumption.
3. India is a top-3 market for the hyperscalers like OpenAI/Microsoft/Google, and announced data center investments total ~$77 billion through 2030, with power demand from Indian data centers projected to grow at a 33% CAGR through 2030. 
4. Industrial and Manufacturing activity under PLI schemes and China +1 strategy adds to the demand.

FY26 saw power demand decline ~0.7% due to the La Niña (weather condition with prolonged rain and winter) — a one-off, not a structural reversal. Recovery to ~5%  demand growth is expected from May 2026 onward on a very supportive base, aligning with India's medium-term 1x real GDP growth multiplier for power demand (Bernstein report).

India is adding capacity across all methods of power generation. On renewables, India added a record ~55 GW in FY26, though additions are expected to moderate to ~35 GW in FY27 as grid constraints and slow tendering bite. 

The SHANTI Bill (nuclear energy) will allow private sector participation and remove recourse on equipment suppliers. NTPC has already issued a global expression of interest for ~15 GW of large PWR nuclear plants. 

BESS(Battery Energy Storage Solution) is finally transitioning from tendering (~31 GWh tendered) to commissioning — ~6 GW is expected to come online in CY26, which is the critical swing factor determining whether peak shortages persist or ease. 

Thermal is seeing a quiet revival, with ~13 GW of state tenders expected and even renewable-heavy states like Gujarat tendering thermal capacity. Crucially, no meaningful surplus is expected before FY31 — the demand-supply equation stays tight, which is constructive for generators.

The market significantly overpaid for the renewable transition story (RE stocks trading @60-70x P/E). The constraint is simple but widely ignored: Renewable energy is variable; the grid is not (demand, supply, and frequency should match at each point in time. Or the grid collapses). 

Solar generates power only during daylight hours, wind is intermittent — neither can be dispatched on demand. This creates the "duck curve" problem where solar floods midday supply (while thermal plants slows down their turbines), suppresses prices, then drops to zero at peak evening demand, forcing thermal to ramp rapidly. 

Thermal plants cannot simply be switched off and on — cold starts take 6–12 hours, and cycling causes mechanical wear and fuel inefficiency, meaning thermal turbines must be kept spinning even at RE peak. Curtailment hit a new high of ~1,000 MU in October 2025 alone — paradoxically, not because of too much power, but because transmission networks cannot evacuate RE fast enough. Transmission target for FY26 was revised down from 24,000 ckm to 15,400 ckm and even that is running at 44% achievement. 

The practical implication is that India needs RE and thermal and storage to run a stable grid — this is not an either/or story, and any portfolio concentrated purely in RE names is exposed to curtailment risk, transmission delays, and margin compression from an impending solar PV cell supply.

Given this complexity, a diversified basket across the energy value chain is the most appropriate way to position. Generators with diversified mix (NTPC — thermal + nuclear optionality + renewables, trading at 13-14x P/E vs. global peer median of 17x, a clear discount). 

Transmission infrastructure (Power Grid Corp — multi-year transmission capex cycle, cost+ asset base with near-perpetual 16-17% ROE, and BESS opportunity leveraging its large substation footprint, though near-term capitalization challenges warrant patience). 

Power financiers (PFC & REC — trading at ~1x P/B and ~5x forward P/E with >20% ROE and clean asset quality.  

Power exchanges (IEX — a long-term structural beneficiary as RE variability increases spot trading volumes, though regulatory overhang from market coupling and potential transaction fee reduction warrants caution near-term; a position sized for the long-term optionality rather than near-term re-rating).
DISCOM bailout is the key risk to monitor as DISCOMs constitute ~40% of PFC/REC loan books.
Risk of accidents in nuclear power plants.
Supply chain risk for thermal power plants (coal & natural gas)
RE overcapacity suppressing merchant prices.
Nuclear execution timelines stretching beyond market expectations.
Price action and fundamental of the overall power sector looks favourable for entry.

The RBI's 125bps repo rate reduction through CY2025 is the most important macro catalyst for Indian real estate. For every 100bps decline in home loan rates, EMI burden on a ₹50 lakh, 20-year mortgage falls by approximately ₹3,000/month. Along with this, GST 2.0 further expands household disposable income, materially improving affordability for mid-income buyers who had been sitting on the sidelines through the high-rate CY2022–24 period.

India’s commercial real estate market witnessed broad-based buoyancy across office, retail, data centres and logistics. Office absorption across the top eight cities is estimated to exceed 59 MSF, while warehousing and industrial leasing is expected to cross 50 MSF for the third consecutive year - underscoring the sector’s structural growth story. Retail leasing gained traction across prime high streets and malls, while the residential market continued its shift towards lifestyle upgrades, with strong demand for premium and luxury housing.

Nifty Realty index corrected ~40%, and realty stocks are now trading at pre-covid valuations (lower than 5yr median TTM PE). A mix of realty stocks(capital appreciation) and REITs(capital appreciation + huge dividends) make a strong allocation to Realty sector,

REITs and Institutional Capital Are Re-Rating the Sector. Indian REITs delivered low-to-mid 30% returns in 2025 versus negative NIFTY Realty and ~10% NIFTY 50. SEBI's January 2026 reclassification of REITs as equity opens up large passive and active fund flows. Institutional investment into real estate is set to exceed USD 7 billion in 2025, with data centres — now tracking 220 MW of 2026 supply — emerging as a mainstream alternative asset class alongside office.
If interest rates increases, then affordability to buy a home decreases, reducing demand and sales.
Demand from NRIs may reduce if new professionals face visa rejections from high earning countries.
Office supply catchup becoming a vacancy risk if IT/GCC demand softens.
Invest in commercial REITs now (since they arein momentum despite all uncertainities)

India's port infrastructure is a direct, leveraged play on the country's $1tn export target by 2030 and the ongoing China+1 supply chain reconfiguration that is routing manufacturing and trade flows through India. Private port operators, particularly those with pan-India presence across both coasts, are structurally advantaged as cargo volumes increase and pricing power coming to scale players with deeper draft, better hinterland connectivity, and SEZ integration.

Private port operators are now moving beyond pure cargo handling into end-to-end logistics — inland container depots, cold chains, last-mile warehousing, etc. This vertical integration expands revenue per tonne and creates switching costs for large cargo clients.

Governance & Regulatory Risk: Concentrated ownership structures and government counterparty dependence in port concession agreements create regulatory risk — any change in concession terms, tariff caps, or port connectivity policy could impair project economics.
Global Trade Slowdown: A sharper-than-expected US or China slowdown would compress global trade volumes and reduce cargo throughput growth below current assumptions

Government CAPEX running at multi-decade highs with Union Budget FY26 allocation of ₹11.11 lakh crore — has created a sustained demand environment for industrial automation, electrification, and power management companies. The PLI scheme across 14 sectors is driving greenfield manufacturing investment that requires industrial equipment across the full value chain — from motors and drives to switchgear, transformers, and factory automation systems.

Make in India Beneficiary requirements under PLI schemes and government procurement rules are forcing MNCs to localise manufacturing — benefiting Indian operations of global industrial conglomerates over imported equipment. This is a structural margin and volume tailwind for companies with established Indian manufacturing footprints.

Indian capital goods companies trade at premium multiples justified by superior RoCE profiles, order book visibility of 18–24 months, and earnings growth compounding at 20%+. The sector has re-rated significantly since 2022 but earnings growth has kept pace with multiple expansion, leaving valuations stretched. Thus exposure should be limited in select stocks only.

Government CAPEX Execution Risk: A meaningful portion of industrial demand is derived from government-sponsored infrastructure projects. Delays in project awards, budget reallocation pressures (Fiscal deficiet increasing amid rising dollar, lower foreign remittances, elevated oil price for longer time) could compress order inflows below consensus expectations.

Competition from Imports: IND-EU trade deal allows Europian machinery and electrical equipment to enter India without any tariff (~44% to 0%). Thought the tariff elimination is phased in 10 years time(mostly 5-7 yrs), the sector will face headwinds at longer horizon (only id domestic players are unable to deliver export quality products at a cheaper price and reliability).

Valuation Risk: At 50–60x trailing earnings, capital goods stocks leave no room for earnings disappointment — any guidance cut or order book slowdown would trigger sharp derating given how much growth is priced in at current levels.

With more disposable income from tax savings and global tensions making some common international travel less attractive, expect a boom in domestic travel. Demand will be driven by a mix of weddings, business trips, MICE(Meetings, Incentives, Corporate, Exhibition), pilgrimages, and airline crew movement. Moreover, the upcoming consumers'(GenZ) philosophy of YOLO(You Live Only Once) - a mindset that encourages
seizing the moment for adventurous and spontaneous experiences, driving demand for unique trips, solo travel, and ticking off bucket-list items, often fueled by FOMO and a desire to live life fully after the pandemic will be the next leg of growth driver for Indian hotel industry.

Digital consumer economy is in the structural shift from unorganised to organised consumption, from offline to digital commerce, whether it be grocery, electronics , fashion, or any other product/service, people love to get things at their fingertips. India's urban consumption story is being driven by a young, digitally-native population with rising disposable incomes, where convenience and experience overweigh price sensitivity in purchase desicions.

Urban Consumption Slowdown: High urban unemployment among youth and plateauing real wage growth in the organised sector could dampen discretionary food and lifestyle spending — the key revenue driver for consumer platforms.

Regulatory  & Compliance Risk: As an overall, the government always tries to act in best interet of customers, requiring companies catering to direct customers adhere strong complaince with rules, procedures, and quality check. Any non-complaice may not only attract severe penalties but also reduced consumer confidence in that brand.

Competition & Burn Rate Resurgence: Any renewed competitive intensity — particularly from well-capitalised new entrants or international platforms — could force reinvestment in discounting and customer acquisition, reversing the unit economics improvement of the last two years.

Indian telecom is undergoing change from a loss-making, hyper-competitive commodity market into a rational duopoly with pricing power and 5G monetisation on the horizon. The elimination of a functional third competitor — Vodafone-Idea's continued financial distress despite government intervention — has created the conditions for ARPU expansion that the sector has been structurally incapable of achieving for nearly a decade. Bharti Airtel has been the most consistent beneficiary of this industry restructuring, consistently gaining both revenue market share and premium subscribers while its balance sheet has strengthened materially.
Along with the primay business of telecom service, the players are actively diversifying the business by offering digital TV solutions, OTT subscriptions, cloud and data center services, etc.

Vodafone-Idea Revival: A successful capital raise and network reinvestment by Vodafone-Idea — perhaps through renewed government support or a strategic foreign partner — could reintroduce competitive pricing pressure and stall Airtel's ARPU expansion trajectory.

Regulatory Spectrum Policy: Any adverse outcome in spectrum renewal auctions — higher than expected reserve prices, unfavourable sharing conditions, or retroactive license fee demands — could create balance sheet stress and divert capital from shareholder returns.

India dominated low-cost generics. The game is changing. Over the next five years, roughly USD 250 billion worth of global innovator drugs are going off-patent. This "patent cliff" is a massive opportunity. Indian companies are also shifting investments heavily into complex generics, biosimilars, and specialty injectables

The Union Budget 2026-27 marks India's shift from manufacturing low-cost generics to becoming a high-value, global biopharma innovation hub. Fueled by the ₹10,000 crore Biopharma SHAKTI initiative, the government is aggressively funding end-to-end R&D, clinical trial infrastructure, and startup incubation. This coordinated policy push aims to capture 5% of the global market and build a $100 billion biotech industry.

India offers complex surgeries—like oncology, cardiac, and organ transplants—at 10–20% of the cost in the West, with world-class clinical outcomes. Inbound patient volume from the Middle East, Africa, and South Asia provides top hospitals with a highly lucrative, dollar-denominated revenue stream.

The gap between supply and demand in healthcare delivery remains huge. India still has roughly 0.5 beds per 1,000 people compared to the WHO standard of 3. Top-tier, listed hospital chains are the only players with the balance sheets to scale up quality infrastructure. At the same time, rising health insurance penetration is rapidly converting previously unaddressable demand into paying patients for these premium hospitals
Strict regulatory non-compliance, high R&D failure rates, patent cliffs, and supply chain disruptions.

Capital Intensity Risk: Greenfield hospital development requires ₹1–2 crore per bed in construction and equipment cost, with a 3–5 year ramp-up period to profitability — aggressive capacity expansion programs can generate significant near-term free cash flow drag before new facilities reach maturity-level occupancy.

Automobile sector is witnessing a GST-driven volume uplift, an accelerating EV transition, and SUV premiumisation. GST restructuring on vehicles reduced the effective tax rate from 28%+cess to 18% and triggered a 20% YoY vehicle volume surge in late 2025. India overtook Japan to become the world's third-largest automobile market by volume in 2024, with annual sales exceeding 5 million passenger vehicles — and penetration at 34 vehicles per 1,000 people remains far below China's 228 or Brazil's 203, underscoring the structural demand runway.
EV Disruption Risk for ICE Leaders: Companies over-indexed to ICE vehicles without credible EV transition roadmaps face long-term market share erosion risk
Supply chain stress - Semiconductor chips and magnets
El Nino & Rural Slowdown: A below-normal monsoon from June 2026 would compress rural incomes and delay two-wheeler purchase decisions

With India in Infra supercycle, materials being used in construction is in strong structural demand, but there's near-term headwinds from simultaneous capacity expansion by all major cement players. Roads, railways, affordable housing, irrigation, and industrial parks — provides multi-year cement volume demand visibility. India's per-capita cement consumption at approximately ~290 kg (FY25) is well below China's ~1,200 kg at a comparable stage of economic development, and the urbanisation-driven construction boom has a decade or more of structural demand runway.

Overcapacity & Pricing Pressure: The Indian cement industry is adding approximately 100 MT of capacity through 2026–27 — equivalent to 20% of current installed capacity. If demand growth disappoints relative to this supply surge, realisation per tonne could decline materially, compressing EBITDA margins
Real Estate Slowdown Risk: A sharp slowdown in residential real estate — Cement's largest demand segment at approximately 65% of consumption — would be the most damaging scenario for sector volumes

Fuel Cost Volatility: Cement kilns consume significant quantities of pet coke and coal — any supply disruption or price spike in global energy markets directly impacts the variable cost structure of cement production, with limited ability to pass through to customers in a competitive pricing environment.

Infrastructure buildout and energy transition is recovering from a valuation trough created by Chinese import dumping and institutional under-ownership through CY2025. The setup for re-rating is compelling: policy protection has established a domestic price floor, demand is compounding from multiple structural drivers, and balance sheets are getting cleaner.

The government placed a 3-year tax on steel imports (specifically targeting China and Vietnam), which has already slashed imports by 34%. This directly protects the profits of domestic steelmakers. Furthermore, Indians consume only 59 kg of steel per person versus the 233 kg global average. With the government pouring ₹11.11 lakh crore into infrastructure, local steel demand is set for steady growth.

China Resumption Risk: Any easing of China's capacity caps or renewed export promotion would flood global markets with cheap steel and aluminium, compressing prices and threatening the safeguard duty regime's long-term efficacy — this is the single largest tail risk for the sector.

EU Carbon Border Adjustment (CBAM): Full CBAM implementation in 2026 imposes an effective carbon tariff on Indian steel exports to Europe — given India's higher emissions intensity from coking coal-based blast furnaces, this structurally erodes export competitiveness in the European market.
